Online edition licensed 2015 CC BY-SA 4.0'). extracted text of PDF page 159 (printed p.147) gives, as the last paragraph of 6.3 PHONOLOGY immediately before '6.4 GRAMMAR': 'It is safe to assume that primary stress was normally, probably always, on the first syllable, as in neighbouring languages.' -- identical to the reported quote; the text-layer excerpt file matches the PDF. The word 'stress' occurs nowhere else in ch. 6 (PDF pp.157-160). Context read: 6.1 Introduction (PDF p.157, printed p.145) says Yanda is extinct, located by T…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, assumed by analogy with neighbouring western Queensland languages (e.g. Kungkari, ch. 3 sec. 3.2.2 p.26 of the same volume: 'Main stress is on the first vowel of a word').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Yanda. (For Kungkari in the same volume, p.26, Breen notes some stress on later syllables of words of four or more syllables to avoid three unstressed syllables in a row, and on long vowels.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; hedged as 'normally, probably always'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (no phrase/intonation remarks). The statement is an explicit inference by analogy with neighbouring languages, not an observation: Yanda is extinct and known only from Eglinton's 1886 wordlist of ~110 words; Breen says no informant alive in the 1970s knew more than the name and calls the chapter 'necessarily highly speculative' (p.145). Section 6.3 also assumes no phonemic vowel length.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen 1990 ch. 6 treats 'Yanda' as Tindale's language of the head of the Hamilton River north of Warenda (Toolebuc, Lucknow), i.e. Glottolog yand1251 exactly; the only data are Eglinton's 1886 list no. 103 in Curr vol. II. The stress statement is an analogical inference for an extinct language with no recorded speech; if the catalog distinguishes observed from inferred statements, this one should be flagged as inferred.
